title: Personal Password Policy
subtitle: Stop and think before you type
description: Follow-ups on routers and firewalls, then why everyone needs a personal password policy, and a simple way to make strong, unique passwords you never have to memorize.

beats.t: Episode 4, September 8, 2005. ShieldsUP! is up to almost 40 million users...
We passed 38 million the other day.
We got a ton of mail about last week's router episode, so let's start there.

Listener Jeff McDonald made a great point. Remember the corporate Zotob outbreak from Episode 1? If one machine on your network gets infected, a firewall on each machine keeps it from spreading to the others.
Although malware on your machine can turn off your firewall. A firewall on my machine protects me from someone else's infected machine.
Also, the free firewalls are disappearing. Computer Associates just bought Tiny, and Kerio is discontinuing its Server Firewall on September 30. The Kerio Personal Firewall is still available.
ZoneAlarm still has a free version, but it's trying to do everything now. I prefer something small and focused.
Someone also pointed out that the XP SP2 Windows Firewall does warn you when a program tries to open a listening port, like a trojan setting up a server.

beats.title: Listening ports
beats.t: A program that "listens" on a port is waiting for incoming connections, like a server. A trojan that opens a listening port is inviting attackers in. The SP2 firewall asks before allowing it, but it doesn't watch outgoing connections.
Lots of people asked about SmoothWall, from smoothwall.org. It's a free Linux-based firewall that turns an old PC into a serious firewall.
Give an old PC a network card for the Internet, one for your LAN and a third for a real DMZ. It has a web interface, so you don't need to know Linux.
Patrick Norton is a big fan. You do need a spare computer for it.
My recommendation: a NAT router for near-perfect protection from outside attacks, plus the free Kerio Personal Firewall 4.2. It's small, light and well behaved.
I've seen too many problems with system-level software. My advice: a router plus the built-in Windows Firewall on XP SP2. That's a pretty good combination.
I think that's true.
It starts with some surprising advice. Jesper Johansson, a senior Microsoft security program manager, told a conference that the usual corporate rule, "never write down your password," is wrong.
Jesper Johansson, a senior Microsoft security program manager, told a conference that the usual corporate rule, "never write down your password," is wrong.
That seems like good advice, though. People stick passwords on their monitors.
If people can't write passwords down, they choose ones they can remember, and those are weak. That's worse than writing them down.
Bruce Schneier agrees. Write them on a small piece of paper and keep it in your wallet. People already know how to protect what's in their wallet.

beats.title: Bruce Schneier
beats.t: A well-known cryptographer and security writer, and founder of Counterpane Internet Security. His advice: a strong password written down and kept in your wallet beats a weak one you can remember.

So what makes a good password? First, most people never decide on a password policy. A site says "create a password," and they type the first thing that comes to mind. Take five minutes and work out a plan.
The biggest threat is a dictionary attack. Huge word lists circulate online, tens of megabytes of every word you can think of.
So real words, pets' names and people's names get cracked quickly.
Forget it. Mix letters and numbers so the password isn't in any dictionary.

beats.title: Dictionary attack
beats.t: Instead of trying every possible combination, an attacker tries likely ones: words, names and common substitutions. It's fast and works surprisingly often, because people choose memorable passwords.
Here's the plan I suggest. Password managers are nice, but they don't come with you to a friend's house, and if someone gets the master password, they get everything.
My idea: invent your own secret rule for turning a site's domain name into a password.
Take every other letter, capitalize in some pattern, swap letters, mix in a number that means something to you, and add a few fixed random characters.
So for nytimes.com I could weave in my birth year and capitalize every third letter. That's not guessable.
Every site gets a different strong password, and you never have to memorize one. You can work it out again anywhere.
Just don't use any example from this show! And if two people happen to invent the same rule, it doesn't matter. Nobody knows who they are.

beats.title: Why it works
beats.t: Each site gets a unique password, so one stolen password doesn't unlock your other accounts. Only the rule needs remembering. Episode 5 adds a warning: make the rule hard to spot from a single password.
So how do you do your passwords, Steve?
Not as well as I should. I keep a Palm Pilot next to me with my notes. Away from it, I try my usual passwords one after another and hope the site is patient.
Same here. I have high-, medium- and low-security passwords. I don't care much if someone guesses my New York Times password.
That's a good point: not everything needs the same protection.
I've had credit card fraud twice. Most recently, my bank let someone change my mailing address through a web form, and things started shipping to Colorado.
The bank used my mother's maiden name to verify me, and I'd given that same answer as a password hint on another site. That's called repurposing: one site's secret becomes another site's key.
And mothers' maiden names aren't hard to find anyway. Remember Paris Hilton? Her password reminder was her dog's name, which everyone knew.

beats.title: Security questions are weak
beats.t: "Secret" answers like your mother's maiden name or a pet's name are often public or reused across sites. Treat them like passwords: give each site a different made-up answer.

quiz.q: Why did Microsoft's Jesper Johansson and Bruce Schneier say it's OK to write passwords down?
options: Banning it pushes people to choose weak, memorable passwords
quiz.explain: A strong password kept safely in your wallet is better than a weak one you can remember.

options: Guessing passwords from huge lists of real words and names
quiz.explain: Attackers try likely words first. That's why real words and names make terrible passwords.

options: Turn each site's domain name into its password with your own secret rule
quiz.explain: Every site gets a unique, strong password that you can work out again anywhere without memorizing it.

quiz.q: What went wrong in Steve's bank fraud story?
options: His mother's maiden name, used by the bank, was also a password hint on another site
quiz.explain: Repurposing: a secret reused on a less careful site became the key to a more important one.

quiz.q: What did Leo recommend for most people's firewall setup?
options: A NAT router plus the built-in Windows Firewall in XP SP2
quiz.explain: The router blocks inbound attacks, and the SP2 firewall adds protection on each PC without the trouble some third-party firewalls cause.
